title: Hierarchical models
dek: Partial pooling: units share a prior, the prior is estimated from the units. The geometry is plates; the payoff is shrinkage.
story: TB data are nested whether you like it or not: reads in isolates, isolates in patients, patients in households, households in districts, districts in surveys. A pooled GLM pretends the rows are iid. A no-pooling GLM fits a separate parameter in every district and overfits the small ones.

A hierarchical (multilevel, mixed-effects) model puts a distribution over unit-level parameters: θ_j ~ N(μ, τ²), then y_{ij} | θ_j ~ f(θ_j). The data update each θ_j and also estimate μ and τ. Small districts shrink toward μ; large ones keep their identity. That is partial pooling.

In a genomics lab this is how you should think about drug-specific error rates in gDST, lineage effects on resistance, and lab effects on MIC. A star on a dummy-variable coefficient for “Beijing lineage” is often a poorly pooled hierarchical fact.
deepTitle: The model form, and the boundary problem
deep: Random-intercept GLM: g(E[y_{ij} | b_j]) = x_{ij}ᵀβ + b_j, b_j ~ N(0, τ²). Marginalizing the Gaussian random intercept in a nonlinear GLM does not give a GLM; that is why people use PQL, Gauss–Hermite, Laplace, or MCMC.

The LRT for H₀: τ = 0 is a boundary test. The null distribution is not χ²_1; it is a 50:50 mixture of χ²_0 and χ²_1. Software that prints a naïve p-value is wrong in a known direction (anti-conservative).

Bayesian hierarchies need a prior on τ. A prior that piles up at 0 (some improper and some “noninformative” choices) can overshrink. Half-t or exponential priors on scale, and checking by prior predictive, are the adult moves.

Phylogenetic correlation is a hierarchical model with a different covariance: random effects along a tree, or a Gaussian process on SNP distance. Ignoring relatedness and then claiming a lineage effect is the same error as ignoring clusters in a survey.

Partial pooling is the λⱼ geometry; mixed models are the integral over u; several noisy experiments sharing a mean is the eight-sites idea (original district numbers, not a copyrighted table). Those plates are this one, unpacked. The boundary LRT for τ=0 remains the inference trap that software still prints as χ²_1.

formulas.label: Random-intercept GLM
formulas.expression: g(E[y_{ij} | b_j]) = x_{ij}ᵀ β + b_j,   b_j ~ N(0, τ²)
formulas.note: Replace the iid error story with a clustered latent intercept.

formulas.label: Gaussian–Gaussian shrinkage
formulas.expression: E[θ_j | y] = λ_j ȳ_j + (1−λ_j) μ,   λ_j = τ² / (τ² + σ²/n_j)
formulas.note: When n_j is small, λ_j drops and the unit is pulled toward the grand mean.

visual.caption: Partial pooling as nested plates: isolates share a patient, patients share a district, districts share a survey mean. Each level has a variance; ignoring a level dumps that variance into the likelihood as fake independence.

example.title: District FQ-R rates with n_j = 4
example.setup: Four districts report FQ-R among RR-TB: 0/4, 1/5, 3/40, 12/50. A no-pooling analyst quotes 0%, 20%, 7.5%, 24%. A hierarchical Beta-Binomial (or logit-normal) shares strength.

steps.title: No pooling is noisy
steps.body: 0/4 is compatible with a true rate of 2% and with 30%. Publishing 0% as a district fact is how small-n maps lie.

steps.title: Partial pooling
steps.body: A random-intercept logit: logit π_j = μ + b_j, b_j ~ N(0, τ²), y_j ~ Binomial(n_j, π_j). Districts with n = 4 shrink hard toward the survey mean; n = 50 barely moves.

steps.title: What you must still check
steps.body: If district D is a referral hospital, τ² is soaking up a mixture of epidemiology and ascertainment. A covariate for “referral centre” belongs in the mean, not only in the mystery variance.

example.takeaway: Shrinkage is not cheating. It is refusing to treat 0/4 as a different scientific object from 12/50 without a variance model.

choices: Every cluster gets the identical estimate, equal to the grand mean
Unit-level parameters share a distribution, so small units shrink toward a shared mean while large units keep more of their data
check.answer: Unit-level parameters share a distribution, so small units shrink toward a shared mean while large units keep more of their data
check.why: That is the λ_j geometry. Complete pooling is the first wrong choice; no pooling is the second.

whyWrong.You delete small clusters: That throws away data and biases toward large centres.

check.prompt: Testing H₀: τ = 0 with a likelihood ratio in a random-intercept model is irregular because:
choices: τ = 0 is on the boundary of the parameter space, so the null is not a regular χ²_1
Random intercepts are not nested in the fixed-effects model
The MLE of τ is always negative
check.answer: τ = 0 is on the boundary of the parameter space, so the null is not a regular χ²_1
check.why: Variance components cannot be negative. Wilks’ interior-point theorem does not apply. A 50:50 mixture of χ²_0 and χ²_1 is the usual fix for this null.

whyWrong.n is always too small: The issue is geometry of Θ, not n.
whyWrong.Random intercepts are not nested in the: They are nested: τ = 0 recovers no random intercept.

check.prompt: On the nested-plates figure, what scientific mistake is “ignoring a level” making?
choices: It removes the need for a likelihood
It treats correlated units as independent, dumping between-unit variance into fake precision
It converts the model into an LRT automatically
check.answer: It treats correlated units as independent, dumping between-unit variance into fake precision
check.why: That is why SEs collapse when you ignore clustering. The plate is a warning about the likelihood’s independence assumption.

whyWrong.It removes the need for a likelihood: You still have one — a wrong one.
